claim: Subjects (N = 24) performed a speeded perceptual discrimination task whereby they were asked to judge the motion direction of random dot kinematograms (left vs. right), and rate their confidence in each choice on a 9-point scale.
source: Subjects (N = 24) performed a speeded perceptual discrimination task whereby they were asked to judge the motion direction of random dot kinematograms (left vs. right), and rate their confidence in each choice on a 9-point scale (Figure 1A).
evidence: Direct description of the experimental task performed by subjects

claim: Stimulus difficulty (i.e., motion coherence) was held constant across all trials, at individually determined psychophysical thresholds.
source: Stimulus difficulty (i.e., motion coherence) was held constant across all trials, at individually determined psychophysical thresholds.
evidence: Direct statement about experimental design

claim: Subjects indicated their direction decision on average 994 ms (SD = 172 ms) after stimulus onset.
source: We found that on average, subjects indicated their direction decision 994 ms (SD = 172 ms) after stimulus onset and performed correctly on 75% (SD = 5.2%) of the trials.
evidence: Reported behavioral measurement from the experiment

claim: Subjects performed correctly on 75% (SD = 5.2%) of the trials.
source: We found that on average, subjects indicated their direction decision 994 ms (SD = 172 ms) after stimulus onset and performed correctly on 75% (SD = 5.2%) of the trials.
evidence: Reported behavioral measurement from the experiment

claim: Subjects tended to employ the entire rating scale, showing that subjective confidence varied from trial-to-trial despite perceptual evidence remaining constant throughout the task.
source: In providing behavioural confidence reports, subjects tended to employ the entire rating scale, showing that subjective confidence varied from trial-to-trial despite perceptual evidence remaining constant throughout the task (Figure 1B).
evidence: Observation from behavioral data and reference to Figure 1B

claim: Confidence is largely known to scale positively with decision accuracy and negatively with response time.
source: Specifically, confidence is largely known to scale positively with decision accuracy and negatively with response time (Vickers and Packer, 1982; Baranski and Petrusic, 1998), though this relationship is not perfect, and is subject to individual differences (Baranski and Petrusic, 1994; Fleming et al., 2010; Fleming and Dolan, 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: A positive correlation was found between confidence and accuracy (subject-averaged R = 0.30; one-sample t-test, t(23) = 13.9, p<0.001).
source: As expected, we found a positive correlation with accuracy (subject-averaged R = 0.30; one-sample t-test, t(23) = 13.9, p<0.001) (Figure 1C), and a negative correlation with response time (subject-averaged R = −0.27; one-sample t-test, t(23) = −7.8, p<0.001) (Figure 1D).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data with reference to Figure 1C

claim: A negative correlation was found between confidence and response time (subject-averaged R = −0.27; one-sample t-test, t(23) = −7.8, p<0.001).
source: As expected, we found a positive correlation with accuracy (subject-averaged R = 0.30; one-sample t-test, t(23) = 13.9, p<0.001) (Figure 1C), and a negative correlation with response time (subject-averaged R = −0.27; one-sample t-test, t(23) = −7.8, p<0.001) (Figure 1D).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data with reference to Figure 1D

claim: Subjects' confidence ratings were generally reflective of their performance on the perceptual decision task.
source: Thus, subjects' confidence ratings were generally reflective of their performance on the perceptual decision task.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the correlation analyses between confidence and accuracy/RT

claim: A serial autocorrelation regression analysis on confidence ratings accounted for only a minimal fraction of the variance (subject-averaged R2 = 0.07).
source: To test this possibility, we performed a serial autocorrelation regression analysis on a single subject basis, which predicted confidence ratings on the current trial from ratings given on the immediately preceding five trials. On average, this model accounted for only a minimal fraction of the variance in confidence ratings (subject-averaged R2 = 0.07).
evidence: Statistical analysis testing for serial correlations in confidence

claim: No significant correlation was found between subjects' confidence reports on the two experimental blocks consisting of identical sequences of random-dot kinematograms (subject-averaged R = 0.02, one-sample t-test, p=0.44).
source: To this end, we compared subjects' confidence reports on the two experimental blocks (consisting of identical sequences of random-dot kinematograms), and found no significant correlation between these (subject-averaged R = 0.02, one-sample t-test, p=0.44).
evidence: Statistical analysis comparing confidence across identical stimulus blocks

claim: Subjects' reports reflected internal fluctuations in their sense of confidence, which are largely unaccounted for by external factors.
source: Taken together, these results support the hypothesis that subjects' reports reflected internal fluctuations in their sense of confidence, which are largely unaccounted for by external factors.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple control analyses

claim: Discrimination performance (Az) between High and Low confidence trial groups peaked, on average, 708 ms after stimulus onset (SD = 162 ms).
source: We found that discrimination performance (Az) between the two confidence trial groups peaked, on average, 708 ms after stimulus onset (SD = 162 ms, Figure 2A; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for Az locked to the time of rating).
evidence: Result from EEG classifier analysis with reference to Figure 2A

claim: The temporal profile and electrode distribution of confidence-related discriminating activity were consistent with previous work using stand-alone EEG to identify time-resolved signatures of confidence during a face vs. car visual categorisation task.
source: Importantly, both the temporal profile and electrode distribution of confidence-related discriminating activity were consistent with our previous work (Gherman and Philiastides, 2015) where we used stand-alone EEG to identify time-resolved signatures of confidence during a face vs. car visual categorisation task.
evidence: Comparison with prior published work by the same authors

claim: The temporal dynamics of decision confidence can be reliably captured using EEG data acquired inside the MR scanner.
source: Together these observations are an indication that the temporal dynamics of decision confidence can be reliably captured using EEG data acquired inside the MR scanner, and that these early confidence-related signals may generalise across tasks.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from consistency with previous work

claim: Early confidence-related signals may generalise across tasks.
source: Together these observations are an indication that the temporal dynamics of decision confidence can be reliably captured using EEG data acquired inside the MR scanner, and that these early confidence-related signals may generalise across tasks.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from consistency across different experimental paradigms

claim: The mean component amplitudes for Medium-confidence trials were situated between, and significantly different from, those in the High- and Low-confidence trial groups (both p<0.001).
source: We subjected these trials through the same neural generators (i.e., spatial projections) estimated during discrimination of High- vs. Low-confidence trials and, as expected from a graded quantity, found that the mean component amplitudes for Medium-confidence trials were situated between, and significantly different from, those in the High- and Low-confidence trial groups (both p<0.001, Figure 2B).
evidence: Statistical analysis of EEG discriminant components with reference to Figure 2B

claim: Component amplitudes were positively correlated with decision accuracy (one-sample t-test on logistic regression coefficients, t(23)=8.6, p<0.001).
source: We found that component amplitudes were positively correlated with decision accuracy (one-sample t-test on logistic regression coefficients, t(23)=8.6, p<0.001, Figure 2C), and were consistently higher for correct vs. incorrect responses across subjects (t(23)=7.58, p<0.001, Figure 2D), in line with the well-established relationship between confidence and accuracy.
evidence: Statistical analysis of EEG component amplitudes with reference to Figure 2C

claim: Component amplitudes were consistently higher for correct vs. incorrect responses across subjects (t(23)=7.58, p<0.001).
source: We found that component amplitudes were positively correlated with decision accuracy (one-sample t-test on logistic regression coefficients, t(23)=8.6, p<0.001, Figure 2C), and were consistently higher for correct vs. incorrect responses across subjects (t(23)=7.58, p<0.001, Figure 2D), in line with the well-established relationship between confidence and accuracy.
evidence: Statistical analysis of EEG component amplitudes with reference to Figure 2D

claim: Differences between Medium-confidence and High-/Low-confidence component amplitudes remained significant when using only correct trials (both p<0.001).
source: To rule out the possibility that the modulation of discriminant component amplitude by confidence was purely explained by objective performance, we compared component amplitudes for Medium-confidence against High-/Low-confidence using only trials associated with correct responses, and showed that differences between these trial groups remained significant (both p<0.001, Figure 2E).
evidence: Statistical analysis controlling for accuracy with reference to Figure 2E

claim: The same pattern of significant differences was found when repeating the analysis separately on error trials (both p<0.001).
source: The same pattern was found when repeating the analysis separately on error trials (both p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical analysis on error trials

claim: The confidence-related neural component can be dissociated from objective performance.
source: These results indicate that the confidence-related neural component can be dissociated from objective performance, as might be expected from previous reports (Lau and Passingham, 2006; Rounis et al., 2010; Komura et al., 2013; Lak et al., 2014; Fleming and Daw, 2017).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the analyses and supported by citations to prior work

claim: The correlation between stimulus duration and discriminant component amplitudes was weak (subject-averaged R = -.15).
source: However, we found that this correlation was weak (subject-averaged R = -.15), suggesting that our classification results could not have been solely driven by this factor.
evidence: Statistical analysis testing for confounding effects of stimulus duration

claim: Mean discriminant component amplitudes did not differ significantly between High vs. Low prestimulus alpha power groups (paired t-test, p=0.19).
source: To do this, we separated trials into High vs. Low alpha power groups, individually for each subject, and compared the corresponding average discriminant component amplitudes. We found that these did not differ significantly between the two groups (paired t-test, p=0.19, Figure 2F).
evidence: Statistical analysis testing for effects of prestimulus alpha power with reference to Figure 2F

claim: Discriminant component amplitudes for the two identical-stimulus experimental blocks were not significantly correlated (subject-averaged R = 0.02; one-sample t-test, p=0.39).
source: In line with this, discriminant component amplitudes for the two identical-stimulus experimental blocks were not significantly correlated (subject-averaged R = 0.02; one-sample t-test, p=0.39).
evidence: Statistical analysis comparing component amplitudes across identical stimulus blocks

claim: Stronger confidence signals were associated with an increased tendency to repeat the previous choice.
source: Thus, stronger confidence signals were associated with an increased tendency to repeat the previous choice.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the analysis of choice repetition behavior

claim: The race model provided a good fit to the behavioural data (Accuracy: R = 0.76, p<0.001; RT: subject-averaged R = 0.965, all p<=0.0016).
source: Overall, we found that this model provided a good fit to the behavioural data (Accuracy: R = 0.76, p<0.001, Figure 3B; RT: subject-averaged R = 0.965, all p<=0.0016, see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for individual subject fits).
evidence: Statistical assessment of model fit with references to Figure 3B and supplement

claim: The BOLD response increased with reported confidence in the striatum, lateral orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), and ventral anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) during the perceptual decision phase.
source: We found that the BOLD response increased with reported confidence in the striatum, lateral orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), the ventral anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) – areas thought to play a role in human valuation and reward (O'Doherty, 2004; Rushworth et al., 2007; Grabenhorst and Rolls, 2011) – as well as the right anterior middle frontal gyrus, amygdala/hippocampus, and visual association areas.
evidence: fMRI analysis results with citations to prior work on these regions

claim: Negative activations (regions showing increasing BOLD response with decreasing reported confidence) were found in the right supplementary motor area, dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, right inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), and anterior insula/frontal operculum during the perceptual decision phase.
source: Negative activations (i.e., regions showing increasing BOLD response with decreasing reported confidence) were found in the right supplementary motor area, dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, right inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), anterior insula/frontal operculum, in line with previous reports of decision uncertainty near the time of decision (Heereman et al., 2015; Hebart et al., 2016 ).
evidence: fMRI analysis results with citations to prior work

claim: During the metacognitive report stage, negative correlations with confidence ratings were found in extended networks including regions of the rostrolateral prefrontal cortex, middle frontal gyrus, superior frontal gyrus, angular gyrus, precuneus, posterior cingulate cortex (PCC), and regions of the occipital and middle temporal cortices.
source: During the metacognitive report stage of the trial (i.e., 'rating phase', defined as the time window beginning at the onset of the confidence prompt; Figure 4B), we found negative correlations with confidence ratings in extended networks (Supplementary Table 2; Supplementary file 1) which included regions of the rostrolateral prefrontal cortex (bilateral, right lateralised), middle frontal gyrus, superior frontal gyrus (extending along the cortical midline and into the medial prefrontal cortex), orbital regions of the IFG, angular gyrus, precuneus, posterior cingulate cortex (PCC), and regions of the occipital and middle temporal cortices.
evidence: fMRI analysis results with reference to Figure 4B and supplementary tables

claim: Positive correlations with confidence ratings during the rating phase were observed in the striatum, amygdala/hippocampus, and motor cortices.
source: Finally, positive correlations were observed in the striatum and amygdala/hippocampus, as well as motor cortices.
evidence: fMRI analysis results

claim: The EEG-informed fMRI analysis revealed a large cluster in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (VMPFC, peak MNI coordinates [−8 40 – 14]), extending into the subcallosal region and ventral striatum, where the BOLD response correlated positively with the EEG-derived confidence discriminating component.
source: This EEG-informed fMRI analysis revealed a large cluster in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (VMPFC, peak MNI coordinates [−8 40 – 14]), extending into the subcallosal region and ventral striatum, and a smaller cluster in the right precentral gyrus (peak MNI coordinates [30 -20 64]), where the BOLD response correlated positively with the EEG-derived confidence discriminating component (Figure 5).
evidence: fMRI analysis results with reference to Figure 5

claim: A smaller cluster in the right precentral gyrus (peak MNI coordinates [30 -20 64]) showed positive correlation with the EEG-derived confidence discriminating component.
source: This EEG-informed fMRI analysis revealed a large cluster in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (VMPFC, peak MNI coordinates [−8 40 – 14]), extending into the subcallosal region and ventral striatum, and a smaller cluster in the right precentral gyrus (peak MNI coordinates [30 -20 64]), where the BOLD response correlated positively with the EEG-derived confidence discriminating component (Figure 5).
evidence: fMRI analysis results with reference to Figure 5

claim: The VMPFC has been linked to confidence-related processes in value-based, as well as other complex decisions.
source: The VMPFC has been linked to confidence-related processes in value-based, as well as other complex decisions (De Martino et al., 2013; Lebreton et al., 2015), however this region is not typically associated with confidence in perceptual decisions (though see Heereman et al., 2015; Fleming et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior research

claim: The VMPFC is not typically associated with confidence in perceptual decisions.
source: The VMPFC has been linked to confidence-related processes in value-based, as well as other complex decisions (De Martino et al., 2013; Lebreton et al., 2015), however this region is not typically associated with confidence in perceptual decisions (though see Heereman et al., 2015; Fleming et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement about typical findings in the literature with citations

claim: Activity in precuneus/PCC regions has been previously shown to scale with confidence.
source: Notably, activity in these regions has been previously shown to scale with confidence (De Martino et al., 2013; White et al., 2014) and hypothesised to play a role in metacognition (McCurdy et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior research

claim: Clusters in the bilateral orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), left anterior prefrontal cortex (aPFC), and right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) showed increased negative correlation with VMPFC activation during the perceptual decision in the PPI analysis.
source: We found that clusters in the bilateral orbitofrontal cortex (OFC; peak MNI: [16 18 -16] and [−28 28–20]), left anterior prefrontal cortex (aPFC; peak MNI: [−40 46 4]), and right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC; peak MNI: [48 22 30]) (Figure 6) showed increased negative correlation with VMPFC activation during the perceptual decision.
evidence: Result from PPI analysis with reference to Figure 6

claim: Regions in the aPFC and dlPFC have been previously linked to perceptual decision making.
source: Interestingly, regions in the aPFC and dlPFC in particular have been previously linked to perceptual decision making (Noppeney et al., 2010; Liu and Pleskac, 2011; Philiastides et al., 2011; Filimon et al., 2013), as well as post-decisional confidence-related processes (Fleming et al., 2012; Hilgenstock et al., 2014; Morales et al., 2018) and metacognition (Fleming et al., 2010; Rounis et al., 2010; McCurdy et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: The temporal and spatial profile of the confidence-discriminating EEG activity were consistent with previous work using a different perceptual task involving face vs. car visual categorisations.
source: We first showed that our EEG results - namely the temporal and spatial profile of the confidence-discriminating activity - were consistent with our previous work (Gherman and Philiastides, 2015) where we used a different perceptual task involving face vs. car visual categorisations, indicating that these confidence-related signals may generalise across a broader range of tasks.
evidence: Comparison with prior published work by the same authors

claim: The spatial topography associated with the confidence-discriminating activity appears consistent with centroparietal scalp projections arising from signals culminating near the decision.
source: Interestingly, the spatial topography associated with this activity appears consistent with centroparietal scalp projections arising from signals culminating near the decision (O'Connell et al., 2012; Kelly and O'Connell, 2013; Philiastides et al., 2014).
evidence: Comparison with prior research on decision-related signals, supported by citations

claim: Distinct neural networks carry information about confidence during perceptual decision vs. explicit confidence reporting stages of the trial.
source: Further, our fMRI data revealed activation patterns suggesting that distinct neural networks carry information about confidence during perceptual decision vs. explicit confidence reporting stages of the trial, respectively.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from fMRI analysis results

claim: Regions showing correlation with confidence during the confidence rating stage, in particular the anterior prefrontal cortex, have been previously associated with explicit metacognitive judgment/report.
source: In contrast, regions showing correlation with confidence during the confidence rating stage, in particular the anterior prefrontal cortex, have been previously associated with explicit metacognitive judgment/report (Fleming et al., 2012; Morales et al., 2018), potentially serving a role in higher-order monitoring and confidence communication.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior research

claim: Neural confidence signals were consistent with predictions from a dynamic model of decision that quantifies confidence as the difference in accumulated evidence in favour of the possible choice alternatives, at the termination of the decision process.
source: Our computational modelling approach provided preliminary insight into the potential decision dynamics that might inform early confidence. Namely, we showed that these neural signals were consistent with predictions from a dynamic model of decision that quantifies confidence as the difference in accumulated evidence in favour of the possible choice alternatives, at the termination of the decision process.
evidence: Result from computational modeling analysis

claim: Early confidence representations could be informed by, yet be distinct from, the quantities reflected in the model-derived confidence.
source: A possible interpretation is that the early confidence representations reflect a readout of this difference (for instance, by a distinct system than the one supporting the perceptual choice itself). In other words, early confidence representations could be informed by, yet be distinct from, the quantities reflected in the model-derived confidence, in line with a dissociation between the information supporting the decision vs. confidence.
evidence: Interpretation of modeling results

claim: Stronger neural confidence signal amplitude increased the likelihood of repeating a choice on the subsequent trial, when the motion direction of the stimulus was consistent with that of the previous trial.
source: In another exploratory analysis that aimed to better understand the potential impact of neural confidence signals on subsequent behaviour, we found that stronger signal amplitude increased the likelihood of repeating a choice on the subsequent trial, when the motion direction of the stimulus was consistent with that of the previous trial.
evidence: Result from behavioral analysis

claim: The VMPFC is not typically known to support perceptual decision processes.
source: Our main fMRI finding, linking early confidence representations with VMPFC activity suggests partial independence of these signals from decision centres. Specifically, as the VMPFC is not typically known to support perceptual decision processes, it seems more plausible that the confidence signals we observe here represent a (potentially noisy) readout of confidence-related information.
evidence: Statement about typical findings in the literature

claim: The confidence signals observed in the VMPFC represent a (potentially noisy) readout of confidence-related information.
source: Our main fMRI finding, linking early confidence representations with VMPFC activity suggests partial independence of these signals from decision centres. Specifically, as the VMPFC is not typically known to support perceptual decision processes, it seems more plausible that the confidence signals we observe here represent a (potentially noisy) readout of confidence-related information.
evidence: Interpretation of fMRI results

claim: Computational and neurobiological accounts of confidence processing have proposed architectures by which a first-level form of confidence in a decision emerges as a natural property of the neural processes that support the decision, and in turn is read out by separate higher-order monitoring network(s).
source: In line with this, computational and neurobiological accounts of confidence processing have proposed architectures by which a first-level form of confidence in a decision emerges as a natural property of the neural processes that support the decision, and in turn is read out (i.e., summarised) by separate higher-order monitoring network(s) (Insabato et al., 2010; Meyniel et al., 2015; Pouget et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to theoretical work

claim: The timing of EEG-derived confidence representations arising in close temporal proximity to the decision (but prior to commitment to a motor response) endorses the hypothesis that the VMPFC may encode an automatic readout of confidence in decision making.
source: The timing of our EEG-derived confidence representations arising in close temporal proximity to the decision (but prior to commitment to a motor response) further endorse the hypothesis that the VMPFC may encode an automatic readout of confidence (Lebreton et al., 2015) in decision making, or early (and automatic) 'feeling of rightness' (Hebscher and Gilboa, 2016) in memory judgments.
evidence: Interpretation of results supported by citations to prior work

claim: Several functional neuroimaging studies have shown positive modulation of VMPFC activation by confidence, across a range of decision making tasks.
source: Consistent with a role in providing a confidence readout, recent work suggests the VMPFC may encode confidence in a task-independent and possibly domain-general manner. Specifically, several functional neuroimaging studies have shown positive modulation of VMPFC activation by confidence, across a range of decision making tasks (Rolls et al., 2010; De Martino et al., 2013; Heereman et al., 2015; Lebreton et al., 2015; Fleming et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: One study showed that fMRI activation in the VMPFC was modulated by confidence across four different tasks involving both value-based and non-value based rating judgments.
source: Notably, one study showed that fMRI activation in the VMPFC was modulated by confidence across four different tasks involving both value-based and non-value based rating judgments (Lebreton et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to specific prior study

claim: Evidence from memory-related decision making research appears to also implicate the VMPFC in confidence processing.
source: Furthermore, evidence from memory-related decision making research appears to also implicate the VMPFC in confidence processing (Hebscher and Gilboa, 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior research

claim: Recent evidence suggests that choice itself (and corresponding motor-related activity) affects confidence.
source: For instance, recent evidence suggests that choice itself (and corresponding motor-related activity) affects confidence (Fleming et al., 2015; Gajdos et al., 2018) and may help calibrate metacognitive reports (Siedlecka et al., 2016; Fleming and Daw, 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior research

claim: The functional connectivity analysis revealed a strengthening of the link between the VMPFC and frontal areas (notably the aPFC and dlPFC) during the perceptual decision stage of the trial.
source: Interestingly, our functional connectivity analysis revealed a strengthening of the link between the VMPFC and frontal areas (notably the aPFC and dlPFC) during the perceptual decision stage of the trial.
evidence: Result from PPI analysis

claim: The VMPFC is a region known for its involvement in choice-related subjective valuation.
source: The observation that the VMPFC, a region known for its involvement in choice-related subjective valuation (Philiastides et al., 2010; Rangel and Hare, 2010; Bartra et al., 2013; Pisauro et al., 2017) encodes confidence signals during perceptual decisions raises an interesting possibility for interpreting our results.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior research

claim: As an internal measure of performance accuracy, confidence is inherently valuable.
source: Instead, as has been suggested previously (Barron et al., 2015; Lebreton et al., 2015), a likely explanation is that as an internal measure of performance accuracy, confidence is inherently valuable.
evidence: Interpretation supported by citations to prior work

claim: Confidence may represent implicit reward and possibly act as a teaching signal to drive learning.
source: Such a signal may represent implicit reward and possibly act as a teaching signal (Daniel and Pollmann, 2012; Guggenmos et al., 2016; Hebart et al., 2016; Lak et al., 2017) to drive learning.
evidence: Interpretation supported by citations to prior work

claim: Recent work suggests that confidence may be used in the computation of prediction errors.
source: In line with this interpretation, recent work suggests that confidence may be used in the computation of prediction errors (i.e., the difference between expected and currently experienced reward) (Lak et al., 2017; Colizoli et al., 2018), thus guiding a reinforcement-based learning mechanism.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to recent research

claim: Regions in the human mesolimbic dopamine system, namely the striatum and ventral tegmental area, have been shown to encode both anticipation and prediction error related to decision confidence, in the absence of feedback.
source: In particular, regions in the human mesolimbic dopamine system, namely the striatum and ventral tegmental area, have been shown to encode both anticipation and prediction error related to decision confidence, in the absence of feedback (Guggenmos et al., 2016), similarly to what is typically observed during reinforcement learning tasks where feedback is explicit (Preuschoff et al., 2006; Fouragnan et al., 2015; Fouragnan et al., 2017; Fouragnan et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior research

claim: Confidence-related effects in the mesolimbic dopamine system were predictive of subjects' perceptual learning efficiency.
source: Importantly, these effects were predictive of subjects' perceptual learning efficiency.
evidence: Statement about findings from cited research

claim: By employing a simultaneous EEG-fMRI approach, we were able to localise an early representation of confidence in the brain with higher spatiotemporal precision than allowed by fMRI alone.
source: In conclusion, we showed that by employing a simultaneous EEG-fMRI approach, we were able to localise an early representation of confidence in the brain with higher spatiotemporal precision than allowed by fMRI alone.
evidence: Summary conclusion of the study

claim: We provided novel empirical evidence for the encoding of a generalised confidence readout signal in the VMPFC preceding explicit metacognitive report.
source: In doing so, we provided novel empirical evidence for the encoding of a generalised confidence readout signal in the VMPFC preceding explicit metacognitive report.
evidence: Summary conclusion of the study

claim: The study provides a starting point for further investigations into the neural dynamics of confidence formation in the human brain and its interaction with other cognitive processes such as learning, and the decision itself.
source: Our findings provide a starting point for further investigations into the neural dynamics of confidence formation in the human brain and its interaction with other cognitive processes such as learning, and the decision itself.
evidence: Statement about implications of the research

claim: Thirty subjects participated in the simultaneous EEG-fMRI experiment.
source: Thirty subjects participated in the simultaneous EEG-fMRI experiment.
evidence: Description of participant sample

claim: Four subjects were removed from the analysis due to near chance (n = 3) and near ceiling (n = 1) performance on the perceptual discrimination task.
source: Four were subsequently removed from the analysis due to near chance (n = 3) and near ceiling (n = 1) performance, respectively, on the perceptual discrimination task.
evidence: Description of exclusion criteria

claim: One subject was excluded whose confidence reports covered only a limited fraction of the provided rating scale.
source: Additionally, one subject was excluded whose confidence reports covered only a limited fraction of the provided rating scale, thus yielding an insufficient number of trials to be used in the EEG discrimination analysis (see below).
evidence: Description of exclusion criteria

claim: One subject had to be removed due to poor (chance) performance of the EEG decoder.
source: Finally, one subject had to be removed due to poor (chance) performance of the EEG decoder.
evidence: Description of exclusion criteria

claim: All results presented are based on the remaining 24 subjects (age range 20 – 32 years).
source: All results presented here are based on the remaining 24 subjects (age range 20 – 32 years).
evidence: Description of final participant sample

claim: All subjects were right-handed, had normal or corrected to normal vision, and reported no history of neurological problems.
source: All were right-handed, had normal or corrected to normal vision, and reported no history of neurological problems.
evidence: Description of participant characteristics

claim: The study was approved by the College of Science and Engineering Ethics Committee at the University of Glasgow (CSE01355) and informed consent was obtained from all participants.
source: The study was approved by the College of Science and Engineering Ethics Committee at the University of Glasgow (CSE01355) and informed consent was obtained from all participants.
evidence: Statement about ethical approval

claim: The EEG analysis was performed on individual subjects using cross validation, such that in estimating the electrophysiologically-derived measure of confidence, each subject became their own replication unit.
source: While we conducted no explicit power analysis for determining sample size, note that our EEG analysis was performed on individual subjects using cross validation, such that in estimating our electrophysiologically-derived measure of confidence, each subject became their own replication unit (Smith and Little, 2018).
evidence: Description of analytical approach with citation
